title: Internal linkage
recap: An identifier with internal linkage belongs to one translation unit. Another source file may define an identifier with the same name without creating a collision because the two names refer to independent entities.

Namespace-scope const and constexpr variables have internal linkage by default. A namespace-scope non-const variable or function can be given internal linkage with static, although unnamed namespaces are generally preferred when hiding several names.
objectives: Give a non-const global variable internal linkage with static.
Use the same internal variable name independently in two source files.
Give a helper function internal linkage.
Link the translation units through one intentionally external function.
warnings: At namespace scope, static changes linkage; inside a function, static instead changes storage duration.
Do not try to forward declare an internal identifier from another translation unit.
An internal name is still global within its own file, so use it only when file-wide access is justified.
challenge: Give each source file its own static g_offset: 2 in main.cpp and 5 in sensor.cpp. In sensor.cpp, also make applyOffset a static helper and expose sensorReading as the external function main calls. Starting from 10, print both independently adjusted readings.
hints: Place static int g_offset at namespace scope in each source file; these are two independent variables.
In sensor.cpp, static int applyOffset(int reading) should add that file's g_offset.
Leave sensorReading non-static so main.cpp's forward declaration can link to it.

contains:
static int g_offset{ 5 };

static int applyOffset(int reading)
